domain: Risk Assessment / Energy Policy / Public Safety Governance
topic_summary: Analysis of the contested acceptable-risk-for-energy kernel in nuclear power debates. Anti-nuclear and pro-nuclear positions read the same risk substrate differently: catastrophic-tail-dominant framing (weight low-probability-high-consequence events heavily) versus expected-value-dominant framing (aggregate expected harm across probability distribution). Each reading instantiates a structurally different constraint on energy policy.

key_entities: Nuclear power generation infrastructure (reactors, fuel cycle, waste storage)
Anti-nuclear movement (Greenpeace, local opposition groups, post-Fukushima mobilization)
Pro-nuclear advocates (industry, climate-focused technocrats, French/Swedish energy ministries)
Regulatory bodies (NRC, IAEA, national safety authorities)
Alternative energy systems (renewables + storage, fossil fuels as implicit comparison class)
Affected populations (proximate communities, future generations for waste, global climate-affected populations)
key_tensions: Catastrophic-tail-dominant vs expected-value-dominant risk framings (structurally incompatible weighting of low-probability-high-consequence events)
Temporal discounting conflict (immediate operational risk vs long-term waste custody vs climate harm from alternatives)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The shared commitment is that energy systems must not impose unacceptable risk on populations; disagreement centers on how to weight low-probability catastrophic outcomes versus aggregate expected harm.
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Regulatory legitimacy derives from claimed ability to quantify and bound risk; interpretive authority contested between technocratic expected-value frameworks (regulators, industry) and precautionary/catastrophic-focused frameworks (environmental movements, post-accident publics).
commitment_system_recognition.candidate_pattern: Interpretive Flexibility (Pattern 3): regulatory layer absorbs drift through evolving safety standards without surfacing that the underlying risk-weighting kernel remains contested; accidents temporarily destabilize interpretive consensus.

readings.commitment: Low-probability catastrophic events dominate risk calculus; tail outcomes weighted categorically above expected-value aggregation.
readings.authority_grounding: Precautionary principle, Taleb-style fat-tail reasoning, post-Chernobyl/Fukushima empirical update on regulatory failure modes.
readings.expected_structural_delta: Nuclear becomes high-ε snare (catastrophic downside creates asymmetric constraint even at low probability); alternatives preferred even with higher aggregate expected harm; victim set includes hypothetical catastrophe-affected populations with infinitesimal discount.

readings.commitment: Risk assessed via expected value across full probability distribution; deaths-per-TWh aggregated without categorical weighting of accident scenarios.
readings.authority_grounding: Technocratic cost-benefit analysis, actuarial frameworks, regulatory safety engineering standards (defense-in-depth, probabilistic risk assessment).
readings.expected_structural_delta: Nuclear becomes low-ε rope or mountain (operational deaths lower than coal/gas per TWh generated); constraint on deployment is coordination/capital, not safety; victim set limited to measurable operational and waste-exposure populations.

readings.commitment: Risk assessed relative to alternatives in portfolio context; climate harm from fossil displacement and intermittency costs of renewables enter denominator.
readings.authority_grounding: Climate science, systems-level energy modeling (IPCC, IEA), comparative mortality studies (Markandya & Wilkinson 2007, Sovacool et al. 2016).
readings.expected_structural_delta: Nuclear becomes actively beneficial constraint (prevents higher-harm alternatives); climate-affected populations enter victim set of non-deployment; beneficiary structure inverts (nuclear opponents now impose extraction on climate-vulnerable populations).

axiom_contradictions.basis: Catastrophic-tail dominance axiom holds that certain classes of low-probability events cannot be aggregated into expected value due to non-linearities in harm (existential risk, irreversible contamination). Expected-value axiom holds that all probabilistic outcomes sum linearly. No single coherent framework can hold both: accepting tail dominance requires rejecting expected-value sufficiency for policy; accepting expected-value sufficiency requires rejecting categorical weighting of tail events.

Tail-dominance axiom treats nuclear catastrophe as categorically unacceptable regardless of alternative harms. Comparative-harm axiom treats all energy-system harms as commensurable within a portfolio optimization. No single framework can hold both: comparative reasoning requires rejecting categorical inadmissibility; categorical inadmissibility requires rejecting harm-commensurability across energy sources.

omegas.description: Are these three readings stable under empirical update? Fukushima shifted German public from expected_value to catastrophic_tail reading overnight. Does accident frequency determine reading selection (empirical) or do readings pre-exist and select confirming evidence (interpretive commitment)?

Does comparative_harm_reading's victim inversion (climate-affected populations as victims of non-deployment) hold if renewables + storage achieve full substitution? If so, the reading's extractiveness depends on technological trajectory not captured in current ε assessment.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) applied to comparative_harm_reading

omegas.description: Where is the threshold between tail-dominant and expected-value-aggregable events? Is 10^-5 per reactor-year (current core damage frequency) below the tail threshold or within it? The readings provide no principle for distinguishing.
omegas.source: Independence testing between catastrophic_tail_reading and expected_value_reading
